title: Discernment is the way (2.26–2.28)
hook: the cure is to tell the seer from the seen, not once in a flash but steadily, and the limbs of yoga make the light grow

segments.voice: Yesterday: apavarga, and your line, for the seer: the world is there for experience and liberation, both. Today, the cure and the remedy.

Identical twins walk into a room. Strangers mix them up all evening. Their teacher gets it right most days. Their mother never gets it wrong, not even from behind, not even half asleep. She didn't learn that in one moment of insight. She learned it over years of ordinary mornings, until telling them apart stopped being an effort and became the way she sees. Patanjali has named the disease and its cause. Today, the cure and the remedy, and the remedy works a lot like that mother's eyes.
screen: `IDENTICAL TWINS.` → `STRANGERS MIX THEM UP.` → `THEIR MOTHER NEVER DOES.`

segments.voice: First the cure. Sutras 2.23 to 2.25 trace the knot: the seer and the seen are joined because of avidya, not seeing clearly. Take away the not-seeing, and the joining falls apart. Patanjali calls that the seer's aloneness. Freedom. Then sutra 2.26 gives the remedy: viveka-khyati, aviplava. Viveka is discernment, telling one thing from another, the way a jeweler tells gold from brass. Khyati is the clear seeing of it. And aviplava is the word to hold: unwavering. Not a flash on a mountaintop that's gone by Monday. Steady. The mother's eyes, not the stranger's lucky guess. Sutra 2.27 says that for one with this steady discernment, wisdom arrives in seven stages, all the way to the end. The sutra doesn't list them; the classical commentary does. Then 2.28 sets up the rest of the book. By practicing the limbs of yoga, impurity dwindles, and the light of knowledge shines brighter, all the way to discernment. A lamp with a sooty glass doesn't need more flame. It needs the glass wiped, again and again. So the eight limbs that start tomorrow aren't rules for their own sake. They're how the glass gets wiped. Day to day, viveka is small and practical: this is a thought, not a fact. This is my mood, not who I am. Said once, it's a flash. Said every day, it becomes how you see.
screen: `THE CURE: NO MORE NOT-SEEING.` · `VIVEKA — TELLING APART.` · `AVIPLAVA — UNWAVERING.` · `THE LIMBS WIPE THE SOOTY GLASS.` · then, large: `VIVEKA.`

segments.voice: Count the out-breaths from one to ten, then start again. When a thought pulls you off count, notice it plainly, a thought, not a fact, and go back to one. Losing count isn't failure: noticing is the discernment, and coming back, again and again, is the steadiness.
Aviplava. Unwavering discernment between seer and seen, held so steady it stops wavering.
Your line: viveka. The mother's eyes, steady every morning, not the stranger's lucky guess. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, discernment between awareness and what it is aware of is the central means of liberation, cultivated over years through study, the ethical disciplines and meditation, usually under a teacher's guidance.

fork.setup: you've had a moment of seeing clearly: you are not your passing moods. by Monday it's faded. what does Patanjali point you to?
options: decide the first one was fake.
practice the limbs until the seeing stops wavering.
fork.reveal: 2.26 asks for unwavering discernment, and 2.28 says it grows by practicing the limbs of yoga as impurity dwindles.

original.note: Sanskrit viveka: discernment, discrimination, telling one thing from another; in 2.26, viveka-khyāti.

trapdoor: what you thought: discernment means good taste or careful judgment.
what it means: telling the seer from the seen, held so steadily it never wavers, is the remedy for suffering.
what a scholar hears: viveka-khyatir aviplava hanopayah (2.26), the remedy that completes the medical fourfold; 2.28 makes the eight limbs the means of that discernment.
recall: one-pointed: a mind on a single object

chat.says: I had one big moment of clarity. Isn't that enough to be free?
options: Patanjali's remedy is aviplava: discernment that stays unwavering, not a flash that fades.
Yes. One flash of clarity is all it takes, and it stays with you for good.
No. Clarity doesn't matter at all; only keeping the rules sets you free.
chat.meaning: Sutra 2.26: the means of removal is viveka-khyati, aviplava: discernment that is unwavering. Steady, like the mother's eyes, not a passing flash.

viveka.meaning: discernment: telling one thing from another

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 2.23–2.25 (avidya causes the conjunction; its removal is the seer's aloneness)
Yoga Sutra 2.26 (unwavering discriminative discernment is the means of removal)
Yoga Sutra 2.27–2.28 (sevenfold wisdom; the limbs of yoga and the light of knowledge)

notes: Sanskrit of 2.26 given as viveka-khyatir aviplava hanopayah; confirm.
The sooty lamp-glass image is the script's illustration, not a quotation from the commentary.
The seven stages of 2.27 are listed in the Yoga Bhashya; not named in the script to keep one idea.
